title: Heat balance: where the energy goes
goal: Explain why most of the energy of exercise becomes heat, write the heat balance equation, and work out how much heat a rider makes in an hour.

steps.title: Most of the energy becomes heat
steps.text:
Muscles are poor engines. Of the energy released from fuel, only a small part ends up as work on the pedals: [gross efficiency](g:gross-efficiency) in cycling is about 20%. The rest, **more than 75%**, is released as heat [[c:hb-heat-75]].

So a rider pushing 250 W on the pedals burns about 1,250 W of fuel and makes about 1,000 W of heat: ten bright old-style light bulbs inside the body.

Running on the flat is even more extreme. Each stride's push and braking cancel out, so the *external* work is about zero and nearly all the metabolic energy ends up as heat in the body [[c:hb-running-zero-work]].

claims.text: More than 75% of the energy from substrate oxidation in muscle is released as heat.

evidence.quote: As a result of the inefficiency of metabolic transfer, >75% of the energy that is generated by skeletal muscle substrate oxidation is liberated as heat.

claims.text: External work is about zero when running on flat ground, so nearly all metabolic energy becomes heat.

evidence.quote: External work is ~0 W when running on a flat surface, as the propulsion and braking forces of gait lead to equal amounts of positive and negative work, respectively

steps.title: The heat balance equation
steps.text:
Physiologists keep the books with one line, the [heat balance equation](g:heat-balance) [[c:hb-equation-terms]]:

**S = M − W − R − C − K − E**

| term | meaning |
|---|---|
| M | metabolic energy used |
| W | external work (power on the pedals) |
| R, C, K | heat lost by [radiation](g:thermal-radiation), [convection](g:convection), [conduction](g:conduction) |
| E | heat lost by evaporation of sweat |
| S | [heat storage](g:heat-storage): what is left |

M − W is the heat produced. Everything in watts. If the losses match production, S = 0 and body temperature holds steady. If not, the leftover is stored and you warm up.

claims.text: Heat storage equals metabolic rate minus external work minus heat lost by radiation, convection, conduction and evaporation.

evidence.quote: The fundamental human heat balance equation states S = M − Wk − R − C − K − E W (1) where S is the rate of body heat storage; M is metabolic rate; Wk is external work rate; R, C, and K represent the rates of dry heat transfer via radiation, convection, and conduction, respectively; and E represents the rate of evaporative heat dissipation.

steps.title: How much heat in one hour at 250 W?
steps.problem: A cyclist rides for 1 h at 250 W with a gross efficiency of 20%. How much heat does the body make, in watts and in kJ?
steps: Metabolic power M = mechanical power ÷ efficiency = 250 W ÷ 0.20 = 1,250 W.
Heat produced = M − W = 1,250 − 250 = 1,000 W. (Shortcut: 80% of 1,250 W.)
Energy over the hour: 1,000 W × 3,600 s = 3,600,000 J = 3,600 kJ (860 kcal).
Common slip: taking 80% of the 250 W on the pedals (200 W). Efficiency applies to the fuel burnt, not to the output.

steps.title: Three dry routes, and when they reverse
steps.text:
Radiation, convection and conduction are *dry* routes: they need a temperature difference. Convection and radiation move heat from warm skin to cooler air and surroundings [[c:hb-dry-gradient]]. Riding at 40 km·h⁻¹ makes a strong breeze, so convection is large on the bike and small on a slow climb.

Conduction is usually negligible in exercise; it matters only with long contact with something hot or cold, such as an ice vest [[c:hb-conduction-small]].

The catch: skin in the heat is about 35 °C. When the air or the sun is hotter than the skin, the dry routes run *backwards* and add heat. Then evaporation is the only way out.

claims.text: Convective and radiative heat exchange are driven by the difference between skin temperature and air or mean radiant temperature.

evidence.quote: Convective and radiative heat losses are driven by a temperature difference between the skin surface (t sk ) and ambient air (t a ) (for convection) and mean radiant temperature (t r ) (for radiation).

claims.text: Conduction is negligible in most exercise but matters with prolonged contact with hot or cold objects such as ice vests.

evidence.quote: However, conduction may represent a major source of heat gain/loss during prolonged exposures to objects hotter or colder than skin temperature, for example, postoperative warming blankets ( 30 ), prerace cooling with ice vests ( 44 ), or sleeping outdoors in a poorly insulated sleeping bag.

steps.title: Heat storage and body size
steps.text:
Whatever heat is not lost is stored, and stored heat raises body temperature [[c:hb-storage-inertia]]. At the start of a run storage is high, because sweating and skin blood flow take minutes to rise. Later, losses catch up and core temperature levels off at a new, higher plateau: storage is back to zero.

How much the temperature rises for a given amount of stored heat depends on the body: its mass, surface area and make-up (its *thermal inertia*). The same stored heat warms a 60 kg runner more than an 85 kg rider. So comparing riders on absolute watts of heat can mislead; per kilogram is fairer (more in the next lessons).

claims.text: Cumulative imbalance between heat production and loss is stored, and the resulting core temperature change depends on body mass, surface area and composition.

evidence.quote: Over the duration of a heat exposure, the cumulative imbalance between heat production and heat dissipation leads to body heat storage, but the consequent change in core temperature, which has implications for health and safety in occupational and athletic settings particularly among certain clinical populations, involves a complex interaction between changes in body heat content and the body's morphological characteristics (mass, surface area, and tissue composition) that collectively determine the body's thermal inertia.

points: More than 75% of the energy used in exercise becomes heat; at 20% efficiency a rider making 250 W produces about 1,000 W of heat.
Running on the flat does almost no external work, so nearly all its energy becomes heat.
Heat balance: S = M − W − R − C − K − E, all in watts; S = 0 means a steady body temperature.
Radiation and convection need skin warmer than its surroundings; when air or sun is hotter than skin they add heat, and only evaporation is left.
Stored heat raises temperature less in a bigger body: compare people per kilogram, not in absolute watts.

variants.stem: A rider holds 200 W for an hour. Of the energy released from fuel in her muscles, where does most of it go?

options.text: It is released as heat in the body
options.why: Right: with about 20% gross efficiency, roughly 80% of the energy becomes heat.

options.text: It is turned into work on the pedals
options.why: Only about a fifth becomes mechanical work; muscles are inefficient engines.

options.text: It is stored as new ATP for later
options.why: ATP is a short-lived carrier, rebuilt and spent within seconds; it is not an energy store that builds up.

options.text: It is lost as carbon dioxide in the breath
options.why: CO₂ is a waste product of oxidation, not a form the energy leaves in; the energy leaves as work and heat.

variants.stem: A triathlete's legs use 1,000 W of metabolic power on the bike. Roughly how much of that becomes heat?

options.why: Right: at about 20% efficiency, 200 W goes to the pedals and about 800 W becomes heat.
That is the mechanical part. The heat is the other 80%.
Muscles are far less than 50% efficient; more than 75% of the energy becomes heat.
This is the opposite: heat is by far the largest share of the energy.

variants.stem: A runner and a cyclist both use 1,000 W of metabolic power, the runner on flat ground. Who makes more heat, and why?

options.text: The runner: on the flat, external work is about zero, so nearly all 1,000 W becomes heat
options.why: Right: push-off and braking cancel out over a stride, so almost no energy leaves as external work.

options.text: The cyclist: pedalling is less efficient than running, so more of it becomes heat
options.why: Cycling puts about 20% into external work; flat running puts about none, so running makes more heat.

options.text: Both the same: metabolic power alone sets heat production
options.why: Heat produced is M − W. The work term differs: about 200 W for the cyclist, about 0 W for the runner.

options.text: The cyclist: sitting still on the bike traps more heat in the body
options.why: Position doesn't change heat production; and the bike's airflow actually helps heat loss.

variants.stem: A cyclist rides at 300 W with a gross efficiency of 20%. What is her rate of heat production?

options.why: This takes 80% of the 300 W on the pedals. Efficiency applies to the fuel burnt: first find M = 1,500 W.
That is the whole metabolic power. The 300 W that goes into the pedals isn't heat inside the body.
This divides 300 by 0.80. Divide by the efficiency (0.20) to get M, then subtract the work.

variants.stem: A rider climbs at 200 W with a gross efficiency of 20%. What is his rate of heat production?

options.why: This takes 80% of the 200 W on the pedals. Efficiency applies to the fuel burnt: first find M = 1,000 W.
That is the whole metabolic power. The 200 W that goes into the pedals isn't heat inside the body.
This divides 200 by 0.80. Divide by the efficiency (0.20) to get M, then subtract the work.

variants.stem: In an Ironman bike leg, a triathlete holds 180 W with a gross efficiency of 20%. What is her rate of heat production?

options.why: This takes 80% of the 180 W on the pedals. Efficiency applies to the fuel burnt: first find M = 900 W.
That is the whole metabolic power. The 180 W that goes into the pedals isn't heat inside the body.
This divides 180 by 0.80. Divide by the efficiency (0.20) to get M, then subtract the work.

variants.stem: A runner produces heat at 1,000 W for 1 h. How much heat is that in kJ?

options.why: This multiplies by 60 minutes instead of 3,600 seconds. A watt is a joule per second.
This treats watts as an amount of energy. Watts are a rate: multiply by the time in seconds.
860 is the answer in kcal, not kJ: 3,600 kJ ÷ 4.184 = 860 kcal.

variants.solution: Energy = power × time = 1,000 W × 3,600 s = 3,600,000 J = 3,600 kJ (860 kcal).

variants.stem: A rider produces heat at 800 W for a 2 h ride. How much heat is that in kJ?

options.why: This multiplies by 120 minutes instead of 7,200 seconds. A watt is a joule per second.
This multiplies watts by hours (800 × 2) and calls it kJ. Use seconds: 7,200 s.
That is the heat for one hour only; the ride lasted two.

variants.solution: Energy = power × time = 800 W × 7,200 s = 5,760,000 J = 5,760 kJ (1,377 kcal).

variants.stem: In a 30 min run, a triathlete produces heat at 1,200 W. How much heat is that in kJ?

options.why: This multiplies by 30 minutes instead of 1,800 seconds. A watt is a joule per second.
That is the heat for a full hour; the run lasted half an hour.
516 is the answer in kcal, not kJ: 2,160 kJ ÷ 4.184 = 516 kcal.

variants.solution: Energy = power × time = 1,200 W × 1,800 s = 2,160,000 J = 2,160 kJ (516 kcal).

variants.stem: A marathon runner's skin is at 35 °C; the air is 39 °C under a strong sun. Which route can still take heat out of her body?

options.why: Right: with air and sun hotter than skin, dry routes add heat; only evaporation still removes it.
Convection needs the air cooler than the skin. At 39 °C air it carries heat into the body.
Under strong sun and hot surfaces, radiation is a heat gain, not a loss.
Conduction is tiny in running, and hot tarmac would add heat, not remove it.

variants.stem: A cyclist rides at 40 km·h⁻¹ in 22 °C air, then climbs at 12 km·h⁻¹ in the same air. Which heat-loss route falls most on the climb?

options.text: Convection, because the airflow over the skin drops
options.why: Right: convection rises with air speed. Slower riding means much less airflow.

options.text: Radiation, because the air temperature drops
options.why: The air is the same 22 °C; and radiation depends on surface temperatures, not airflow.

options.text: Conduction, because the hands grip the bars harder
options.why: Conduction through hands and saddle is negligible either way.

options.text: Evaporation, because sweat stops on climbs
options.why: Sweating goes on (often rises) on climbs; it is the airflow that drops.

variants.stem: In which case does conduction carry a large share of heat?

options.text: Wearing an ice vest during a warm-up
options.why: Right: long contact with a cold object is when conduction matters.

options.text: Running a 10 km race on a cool day
options.why: Only the soles touch the ground, briefly: conduction is negligible.

options.text: Riding fast on the flat in summer
options.why: Fast riding is dominated by convection and evaporation, not by contact.

options.text: Sweating heavily in a humid gym
options.why: Sweating is evaporative heat loss, a different route.

variants.stem: Forty minutes into a steady ride, a cyclist's core temperature has levelled off at 38.3 °C. What does that say about her heat balance?

options.text: Heat loss now matches heat production, so storage is about zero
options.why: Right: a steady temperature means S ≈ 0, even though the plateau is above resting.
At steady power she still makes several hundred watts of heat; it is all being lost.

options.text: She is still storing heat at the same rate as at the start
options.why: Storing heat would keep temperature rising. A plateau means storage has fallen to about zero.

options.text: Her body is now losing more heat than it makes
options.why: Then her core temperature would be falling, not steady.

variants.stem: A 58 kg runner and an 85 kg runner both store 300 kJ of heat in the first 20 min of a race. Whose core temperature rises more?

options.text: The 58 kg runner's, because the same heat is spread over less mass
options.why: Right: thermal inertia grows with mass, so the same stored heat warms a small body more.

options.text: The 85 kg runner's, because a bigger body holds more heat
options.why: Holding more heat for the same rise is the point: the bigger body warms less per kJ.

options.text: Both the same, because they stored the same heat
options.why: The temperature change depends on heat stored *and* the body's mass and make-up.

options.text: Whoever is fitter, whatever their mass
options.why: Fitness changes how much heat is made and lost, but here the stored heat is fixed; mass decides the rise.
